claim: Tuberculosis disproportionately affects the Canadian Inuit.
source: Tuberculosis disproportionately affects the Canadian Inuit.
evidence: This is stated as established fact in the abstract without specific data provided in this sentence, drawing on general knowledge of TB epidemiology in Canada.

claim: The outbreak studied occurred in the Arctic during 2011-2012 and comprised 50 cases.
source: using a well-characterized outbreak from the Arctic (2011–2012, 50 cases)
evidence: Direct statement of the outbreak characteristics in the abstract.

claim: Samples were sequenced to approximately 500-1000x depth.
source: Samples were sequenced to ~500–1000x and reads were aligned to a novel local reference genome generated with PacBio SMRT sequencing.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing methodology in the abstract.

claim: A novel local reference genome was generated using PacBio SMRT sequencing.
source: Samples were sequenced to ~500–1000x and reads were aligned to a novel local reference genome generated with PacBio SMRT sequencing.
evidence: Direct statement of methodology in the abstract.

claim: Deep sequencing identified a novel super-spreader who likely transmitted to up to 17 other cases during the outbreak (35% of the remaining cases that year).
source: In contrast with previous genomic analyses using ~50x depth, deep sequencing allowed us to identify a novel super-spreader who likely transmitted to up to 17 other cases during the outbreak (35% of the remaining cases that year).
evidence: Direct statement of the primary finding in the abstract, supported by the deep sequencing data analysis.

claim: Within-host diversity should be incorporated into transmission analyses.
source: It is increasingly evident that within-host diversity should be incorporated into transmission analyses
evidence: Statement drawing on emerging scientific consensus and the findings of this study.

claim: Deep sequencing may facilitate more accurate detection of super-spreaders and transmission clusters.
source: deep sequencing may facilitate more accurate detection of super-spreaders and transmission clusters.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the findings of this study, presented as speculation about broader applicability.

claim: The findings have implications for all genomic studies of transmission regardless of pathogen.
source: This has implications not only for TB, but all genomic studies of transmission - regardless of pathogen.
evidence: Speculative statement about broader implications based on the study findings.

claim: TB in Canada is highest among the Inuit, with a rate over 300 times that of the non-Indigenous Canadian-born population in 2016.
source: Tuberculosis (TB) in Canada is highest among the Inuit, an Indigenous population with a rate over 300 times that of the non-Indigenous Canadian-born population in 2016 (Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, 2018.

claim: Canada set a goal of TB elimination in the Inuit by 2030.
source: Canada recently set a goal of TB elimination in the Inuit by 2030, (Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, 2018.

claim: TB elimination in the Inuit will not be achieved without halting ongoing transmission.
source: Canada recently set a goal of TB elimination in the Inuit by 2030, (Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, 2018) which will not be achieved without halting ongoing transmission.
evidence: Logical inference based on the nature of TB transmission and elimination goals.

claim: Previous studies have used genomic data to investigate TB transmission dynamics in the Canadian North.
source: Previous studies have used genomic data either alone or in conjunction with classical epidemiology to investigate TB transmission dynamics in the Canadian North, (Tyler et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2015a; Lee et al., 2015b)
evidence: Supported by citations to Tyler et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2015a; Lee et al., 2015b.

claim: Previous TB genomic studies in the Canadian North have relied on identifying consensus single nucleotide polymorphisms (cSNPs).
source: Thus far, such studies have relied on identifying consensus single nucleotide polymorphisms (cSNPs), consistent with prevailing methodology in this field.
evidence: Statement about methodology consistent with established practice in the field.

claim: Incorporation of within-host diversity into genomic analyses may provide greater resolution of transmission than cSNP-based approaches alone.
source: Recent studies suggest that incorporation of within-host diversity into genomic analyses may provide greater resolution of transmission than cSNP-based approaches alone (Worby et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2018; Meehan et al., 2019; Séraphin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Worby et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2018; Meehan et al., 2019; Séraphin et al., 2019.

claim: Within-host diversity analysis may be particularly important for investigation of outbreaks occurring over short time scales.
source: This may be particularly important for investigation of outbreaks occurring over short time scales and/or in settings such as the Canadian North, where the genetic diversity of circulating strains is especially low.
evidence: Inference based on the limitations of cSNP approaches in short timeframes.

claim: Within-host diversity analysis may be particularly important in settings where the genetic diversity of circulating strains is especially low.
source: This may be particularly important for investigation of outbreaks occurring over short time scales and/or in settings such as the Canadian North, where the genetic diversity of circulating strains is especially low.
evidence: Inference based on the limitations of cSNP approaches in low diversity settings.

claim: The genetic diversity of circulating TB strains in the Canadian North is especially low.
source: This may be particularly important for investigation of outbreaks occurring over short time scales and/or in settings such as the Canadian North, where the genetic diversity of circulating strains is especially low.
evidence: Statement about the epidemiological context based on established knowledge of TB in this region.

claim: It is common to find many samples separated by zero cSNPs in short time scale outbreaks and low diversity settings.
source: In both of these circumstances, it is common to find many samples separated by zero cSNPs, hindering accurate source ascertainment.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of genomic epidemiology challenges.

claim: Finding many samples separated by zero cSNPs hinders accurate source ascertainment.
source: In both of these circumstances, it is common to find many samples separated by zero cSNPs, hindering accurate source ascertainment.
evidence: Logical inference about the limitations of cSNP-based methods.

claim: The outbreak studied occurred in Nunavik, Québec.

claim: The outbreak has been previously described.
source: This outbreak, which has been previously described, (Lee et al., 2015b; Lee et al., 2016)

claim: M. tuberculosis has a low mutation rate of approximately 0.2-0.3 SNPs/genome/year for Lineage 4.

evidence: Supported by citation to Menardo et al., 2019.

source: All 50 samples from the 2011–2012 outbreak (Lee et al., 2015b) were eligible for inclusion

claim: Three samples could not be re-grown.
source: The remaining three samples could not be re-grown.

source: There were also no hSNPs shared across all 62 samples using MT-0080_PB.

claim: A local reference is important for accurate identification of hSNPs.

source: A population-level genomic epidemiology study is currently underway to evaluate this.
evidence: Statement of ongoing research.

claim: Using a local strain as a reference can reduce error in variant detection.
source: We have shown that using a local strain as a reference can not only reduce error
evidence: Conclusion based on the comparison of H37Rv and MT-0080_PB results.

claim: Using a local strain as a reference improves detection of epidemiologically-informative variants.
source: but improves detection of epidemiologically-informative variants.
evidence: Conclusion based on the comparison of H37Rv and MT-0080_PB results.

claim: Genomic differences between outbreak strains and H37Rv have been previously illustrated.
source: Genomic differences between outbreak strains and H37Rv have been previously illustrated by Roetzer et al. (2013); O'Toole and Gautam (2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Roetzer et al., 2013 and O'Toole and Gautam, 2017.

claim: Clinical TB strains may be needed to fully detect virulence genes in reference-based analyses.
source: with O'Toole and Gautam (2017) warning that clinical TB strains may be needed to fully detect virulence genes in reference-based analyses.
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Toole and Gautam, 2017.

claim: Local reference genomes may be warranted for hSNP analysis.
source: Our analysis suggests these may also be warranted for hSNP analysis
evidence: Inference based on the findings of this study.

claim: Using long-read sequencing to generate complete and local reference genomes is suggested where possible.
source: where possible, we suggest using long-read sequencing to generate complete and local reference genomes.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The study had access to a densely-sampled outbreak.
source: Firstly, we had access to a densely-sampled outbreak
evidence: Statement of study strength.

claim: The outbreak was previously investigated using 'standard' sequencing depth.
source: which was previously investigated using 'standard' sequencing depth
evidence: Statement of study design allowing comparison.

claim: Detailed epidemiological data was available for the outbreak.
source: and for which detailed epidemiological data was available.
evidence: Statement of available data.

claim: The use of long-read data allowed complete assembly of a novel TB genome from Nunavik.
source: Finally, the use of long-read data has allowed us to completely assemble a novel TB genome from Nunavik.
evidence: Direct statement of methodological achievement.

claim: The novel TB genome from Nunavik will serve as a valuable resource for future studies of transmission in Nunavik.
source: This will serve as a valuable resource for future studies of transmission in Nunavik (given the low strain diversity in the region Lee et al., 2015a)
evidence: Speculation about future utility, with citation supporting the context of low diversity.

claim: The novel TB genome from Nunavik will serve as a valuable resource for other Inuit territories.
source: as well as other Inuit territories.
evidence: Speculation about broader utility.

claim: Deep sequencing in this study was done using DNA extracted from culture due to the historical nature of the outbreak.
source: A potential limitation of this work is that, given the historical nature of the outbreak, deep sequencing was done using DNA extracted from culture.
evidence: Statement of methodological limitation.

claim: Few studies have examined the effect of culture on genome diversity due to methodological challenges of sequencing directly from sputum.
source: Due to methodological challenges of sequencing directly from sputum, (Brown et al., 2015; Votintseva et al., 2017; Doyle et al., 2018) few studies have examined the effect of culture on genome diversity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 2015; Votintseva et al., 2017; Doyle et al., 2018.

claim: A study by Shockey et al. (2019) suggests that some diversity may be lost during the culturing process.
source: A recent study by Shockey et al. (2019)., which analyzed allelic variation among reads from individual samples, suggests that some diversity may be lost during the culturing process.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shockey et al., 2019.

claim: Several studies found results were congruent between cSNP analyses from culture versus raw samples.
source: However, several studies looking at potential transmission (Votintseva et al., 2017; Doyle et al., 2018; Nimmo et al., 2019) found results were congruent between cSNP analyses from culture versus raw samples.
evidence: Supported by citations to Votintseva et al., 2017; Doyle et al., 2018; Nimmo et al., 2019.

claim: Studies reported detecting fewer hSNPs with sequencing from culture versus from sputum.
source: In terms of hSNPs, Votintseva et al. (2017) Doyle et al. (2018); Nimmo et al. (2019) reported detecting fewer hSNPs with sequencing from culture versus from sputum
evidence: Supported by citations to Votintseva et al., 2017; Doyle et al., 2018; Nimmo et al., 2019.

claim: In Nimmo et al. (2019), the median hSNPs was 4.5 with culture versus 5 hSNPs with sputum.
source: in Nimmo et al. (2019), the median hSNPs was only 4.5 versus 5 hSNPs, respectively
evidence: Supported by citation to Nimmo et al., 2019.

claim: The difference in hSNPs between culture and sputum may not be clinically significant, regardless of statistical significance.
source: a difference that may not be clinically significant, regardless of statistical significance.
evidence: Interpretation of the cited findings.

claim: Further study is needed to understand how hSNP diversity may be affected by the culturing process.
source: Given the inconsistency of results and paucity of data, further study is needed to understand how hSNP diversity may be affected by the culturing process
evidence: Statement of research need based on literature review.

claim: Further study is needed to assess whether culturing affects inferences of transmission.
source: and to assess whether this affects inferences of transmission.
evidence: Statement of research need.

claim: Enhanced detection of hSNPs present in sputum would likely improve the resolution over that presented in this work.
source: We note that it is likely that enhanced detection of the hSNPs present in sputum would improve the resolution over that which we present in this work.
evidence: Speculation about potential improvements.

claim: The sequencing data and bioinformatics pipelines between the previous analysis and deep sequencing analysis are not directly comparable.
source: Another potential limitation is that, while we can compare the epidemiological inferences made between our previous analysis and our deep sequencing analysis, the sequencing data and bioinformatics pipelines themselves are not directly comparable.
evidence: Statement of methodological limitation.

claim: Methods to accurately identify hSNPs and incorporate them into transmission analyses are currently an area of active research.
source: Methods to accurately identify hSNPs and incorporate them into transmission analyses are currently an area of active research.
evidence: Statement of current state of the field.

claim: Additional steps and strict thresholds must be used to minimize false positive hSNPs.
source: We illustrated in our recent paper (Martin et al., 2018) that additional steps and strict thresholds must be used to minimize false positive hSNPs
evidence: Supported by citation to Martin et al., 2018.

claim: In the 2015 analysis, MT-504 had five reference alleles at position 276,685 in the H37Rv alignment (out of 75).
source: However, we note that pre-filtering, our 2015 analysis found that MT-504 had five reference alleles at position 276,685 in the H37Rv alignment (out of 75)
evidence: Statement of previous analysis results.

claim: Randomly downsampling the current data to simulate ~50x yielded similar results (5/47 reads at position 276,544 aligned to MT-0080_PB).
source: and randomly downsampling the current data to simulate ~50 x yielded similar results (5/47 reads at position 276,544 aligned to MT-0080_PB).
evidence: Direct statement of downsampling experiment results.

claim: Most genomic studies of TB employ conservative thresholds of 75-90% allele frequency to classify cSNPs.
source: As most genomic studies of TB employ conservative thresholds of 75–90% allele frequency to classify cSNPs
evidence: Statement of common practice in the field.

claim: Many bioinformatics pipelines would consider heterogeneity at ~19% allele frequency as potentially suspect at standard sequencing depth.
source: many bioinformatics pipelines would consider this heterogeneity as potentially suspect at standard sequencing depth.
evidence: Inference about how standard pipelines would handle the observed heterogeneity.

claim: Greater depth and/or different analytic approaches are needed to ensure accurate discrimination of sequencing/analytic error from true variation.
source: This suggests that greater depth and/or different analytic approaches (e.g., Wyllie et al., 2019) are needed to ensure accurate discrimination of sequencing/analytic error from true variation
evidence: Inference based on the findings, with citation to alternative approach.

claim: The optimal approach used to identify variants needs to be carefully considered and appropriate for the study question and data being analyzed.
source: ultimately, the optimal approach used to identify variants needs to be carefully considered, and appropriate for the study question and data being analyzed.
evidence: General methodological recommendation.

claim: Deep sequencing may not always be necessary to detect super-spreading events.
source: Finally, while deep sequencing allowed us to detect a novel superspreading event in this context, this approach may not always be necessary; indeed, our previous analysis had identified another super-spreader in the same outbreak using routine sequencing.
evidence: Statement acknowledging limitations of generalizability.

claim: The Northern outbreak may not be representative of outbreaks from other settings and/or involving other M. tuberculosis lineages.
source: We acknowledge that this Northern outbreak may not be representative of outbreaks from other settings and/or involving other M. tuberculosis lineages.
evidence: Statement of limitation regarding generalizability.

claim: Further studies are needed to quantify the degree to which super-spreading occurs in TB.
source: Further studies are needed to quantify the degree to which super-spreading occurs in TB, and examine how and when deep sequencing should be used to detect this.
evidence: Statement of research need.

claim: Further studies are needed to examine how and when deep sequencing should be used to detect super-spreading.
source: Further studies are needed to quantify the degree to which super-spreading occurs in TB, and examine how and when deep sequencing should be used to detect this.
evidence: Statement of research need.

claim: Evidence was found of mixed variants with important epidemiologic implications that would not have been detected with standard methods and common filtering criteria.
source: In summary, we have found evidence of mixed variants with important epidemiologic implications that would not have been detected with standard methods and common filtering criteria.
evidence: Summary statement of key finding.

claim: No other studies have been published comparing epidemiological inferences obtained with deep versus routine sequencing for TB outbreak resolution.
source: To our knowledge, however, no other studies have been published comparing epidemiological inferences obtained with deep versus routine sequencing for TB outbreak resolution
evidence: Statement of novelty based on literature review.

claim: This work represents an important methodological advance in TB genomic epidemiology.
source: thus this work represents an important methodological advance in this area.
evidence: Claim about the significance of the work.

claim: Genomic methods still require careful interpretation and can harbor considerable ambiguity when comparing very close links in a transmission chain.
source: We illustrate that genomic methods, while powerful, still require careful interpretation and can still harbor considerable ambiguity when comparing very close links in a transmission chain
evidence: Conclusion about limitations of genomic methods.

claim: Genomic methods can harbor considerable ambiguity when trying to identify source cases.
source: or, as also suggested in Xu et al. (2019), when trying to identify source cases.
evidence: Conclusion about limitations, supported by citation to Xu et al., 2019.

claim: The finding about genomic method limitations is likely relevant beyond TB, given the increasing number of pathogens undergoing genomic investigation.
source: This finding is likely relevant beyond TB, given the increasing number of pathogens undergoing genomic investigation.
evidence: Speculation about broader relevance.

claim: Reproducing previous genomic epidemiology analyses is important.
source: Our work also highlights the importance of reproducing previous genomic epidemiology analyses
evidence: Recommendation based on the study experience.

claim: As technology and methods in genomic epidemiology continue to develop, these can lead to improved resolution of transmission.
source: as the technology and methods used in this field continue to develop, these can lead to improved resolution of transmission
evidence: Statement about the evolving nature of the field.

claim: Developing technology and methods can challenge previously-held inferences with critical implications for public health.
source: and ultimately, challenge previously-held inferences – with critical implications for public health.
evidence: Inference about the impact of methodological advances.

claim: Deep sequencing can aid in transmission analyses, particularly by allowing accurate identification of TB super-spreading events and associated epidemiological characteristics.
source: In terms of TB control, we demonstrate that deep sequencing can aid in transmission analyses, in particular by allowing accurate identification of TB super-spreading events and associated epidemiological characteristics.
evidence: Summary of key finding and its implications.

claim: Deep sequencing is most useful for understanding transmission in settings with low strain diversity.
source: We propose that deep sequencing is most useful for understanding transmission in settings with low strain diversity
evidence: Proposal based on the study findings.

claim: Settings with low strain diversity may benefit from routine use of deep sequencing.
source: and that these may benefit from routine use of this approach.
evidence: Recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Deep sequencing may provide additional resolution of transmission events within outbreaks occurring over short, limited timescales, irrespective of local strain diversity.
source: We hypothesize deep sequencing may also provide additional resolution of transmission events within outbreaks occurring over short, limited timescales – irrespective of local strain diversity, as (by definition) all samples involved in recent transmission would be expected to be closely-related.
evidence: Hypothesis about broader applicability.

claim: Further studies comparing deep versus routine sequencing from a diversity of clusters and epidemiologic contexts are needed to fully quantify the added value of deep sequencing for epidemiologic studies of TB.
source: However, further studies comparing deep versus routine sequencing, ideally from a diversity of clusters and epidemiologic contexts, are needed to fully quantify the added value of this approach for epidemiologic studies of TB.
evidence: Statement of research need.

claim: This work has important implications for the Canadian North and other regions with high TB transmission.
source: Overall, this work has important implications for the Canadian North, as well as other regions with high TB transmission
evidence: Statement about the broader significance of the work.

claim: As next-generation sequencing becomes a mainstay in public health surveillance, it is critical to recognize the limitations of analyses done using routine sequencing data.
source: as next-generation sequencing becomes a mainstay in public health surveillance, it is critical we recognize the limitations of analyses done using routine sequencing data.
evidence: Recommendation about public health practice.

claim: Accurate resolution of transmission is essential for TB control programmes.
source: Accurate resolution of transmission is essential for TB control programmes
evidence: Statement of public health principle.

claim: Accurate resolution of transmission enables better understanding of risk factors for transmission and prioritization of public health resources.
source: in order to better understand risk factors for such transmission and enable prioritization of public health resources.
evidence: Statement of public health rationale.

claim: The findings were regarded as very valuable by the regional public health unit and local community leaders in Nunavik.
source: With respect to Nunavik, our findings were regarded as very valuable by the regional public health unit and local community leaders
evidence: Statement of stakeholder response.

claim: As a direct consequence of this work, ongoing and new investigations of TB genomic epidemiology in Nunavik are using deep sequencing to inform transmission analyses.
source: as a direct consequence of this work, ongoing and new investigations of TB genomic epidemiology in Nunavik are using deep sequencing to inform transmission analyses.
evidence: Statement of impact on public health practice.

claim: Deep sequencing of all samples in an outbreak may not be economically viable in every setting.
source: However, while costs continue to decline, we recognize deep sequencing of all samples in an outbreak may not be economically viable in every setting.
evidence: Acknowledgment of practical limitations.
